blocks.title: Purpose of satire
blocks.text: Satire uses humor, irony, exaggeration, or ridicule to expose a social flaw and invite judgment. Its aim is not merely to entertain: the comic surface directs attention toward a target such as hypocrisy, corruption, vanity, or an unjust institution.

blocks.title: Literal statement and implied critique
blocks.text: Verbal irony creates a gap between the words a speaker states and the meaning an audience is expected to infer. A satirist may sound as though an absurd policy deserves praise, while contextual contradictions signal that the apparent praise is actually criticism.

blocks.title: Exaggeration
blocks.text: Exaggeration stretches a real tendency beyond ordinary limits so its consequences become difficult to ignore. The distortion works when readers can still recognize the underlying behavior; random absurdity without a recognizable target does not create effective critique.

blocks.title: Audience inference
blocks.text: Indirect criticism asks readers to connect the comic surface to the real target themselves. That act of inference can make the judgment more memorable and can reduce immediate resistance because the text demonstrates a contradiction instead of announcing a conclusion as a lecture.

blocks.title: Context and shared knowledge
blocks.text: A satirical statement depends on context. Readers need enough shared knowledge to notice that the literal claim conflicts with known values, events, or consequences. Without those signals, sincere readers may mistake the surface statement for the author's actual position.

blocks.title: Parody and satire
blocks.text: Parody imitates the style of a recognizable work, speaker, or genre. Parody becomes satirical when that imitation exposes a broader weakness or abuse; imitation by itself may be playful without making a social criticism.

blocks.title: Tone is not the position
blocks.text: A calm or enthusiastic narrator can voice an outrageous proposal without endorsing it. To interpret the passage, distinguish the narrator's performed tone from the author's critical design and test whether details consistently reveal harmful or contradictory consequences.

blocks.title: Analyzing a new case
blocks.text: To analyze an unfamiliar satire, identify the literal claim, the target, the contradiction that makes the claim unstable, and the judgment the audience is invited to form. Evidence for the interpretation should come from specific wording and context rather than from labeling every joke as satire.
